added_claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
added_claims.quote: It's also it's up 20% or so over the past 12 months
added_claims.claim: The SG CTA index was up about 15.7% through September 2026 and about 20% over the trailing 12 months, one of the best 12-month stretches Beer has seen, which cuts against the reputation that the space gives back each good year.
added_claims.conditions: 2026 had several competing themes rather than one

added_claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
added_claims.quote: the pendulum swung too far to the easy answer which was 60/40 between stocks and bonds and everybody got benchmarked to it
added_claims.claim: Benchmarking everyone to 60/40 turned a simple rule into industry-wide herding; because it worked again and again, the framework swung too far to one answer and now faces an existential crisis.
added_claims.conditions: long period of negative stock-bond correlation
added_claims.testable: partly - herding is hard to measure directly

added_claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
added_claims.quote: I don't want to throw out the whole construct because I need a framework to work with and and the moment I throw out the construct and start with something completely new guess what that's not going to work either
added_claims.claim: Allocators will not discard the 60/40 framework (a framework is needed and a brand-new one would also fail), so the realistic path to growth for CTAs is incremental change at the margin, replacing part of the 40.
added_claims.direction: gradual shift from bonds to alternatives

added_claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
added_claims.quote: I really can't predict what's going to happen over the next 3 months but I'm very confident what's going to happen over the next 10 years
added_claims.claim: Strategic asset allocation implicitly assumes more predictability over ten years than over three months, which he calls a little crazy; the rationale is behavioral discipline, not forecasting skill.
added_claims.testable: partly - CMA forecast error is measurable

added_claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
added_claims.quote: these poor retail investors are doing everything at the wrong time. They're buying at the top and selling at the bottom
added_claims.claim: Investor-return studies (Morningstar) show retail investors buy tops and sell bottoms, the empirical base for the asset-allocation ethos of diversifying and not trading tactically.
added_claims.direction: investors underperform the funds they hold

added_claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
added_claims.quote: when we define crisis, we mean an equity bare market
added_claims.claim: Crisis alpha is judged only against equity bear markets, because equities drive growth in nearly every portfolio; a commodity decline does not hurt the whole portfolio, so only equity drawdowns count as crises.
added_claims.conditions: three sustained crises in 27 years plus a minor one in 2022
added_claims.testable: yes - define crisis windows by equity drawdown

added_claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
added_claims.quote: if you can get 50 to 150 basis points of alpha generation in your portfolio from bonds
added_claims.claim: Even in the bond bull market, 50-150 bp of alpha versus equities was a win for bonds, and gold's 9% alpha is mostly its recent surge; CTAs' 330 bp is at the top of the range, so alpha comparison favors CTAs.
added_claims.indicator: alpha vs S&P 500 by asset class
added_claims.testable: yes - regress each asset class on S&P 500

added_claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
added_claims.quote: they're insurance. You pay pay and hope you make a lot of money back
added_claims.claim: Volatility and other crisis hedges are insurance (you pay a premium and hope), which is psychologically hard to hold, while CTAs protect in crises and also have a positive long-run Sharpe.
added_claims.indicator: carry cost of tail hedges vs trend crisis alpha
added_claims.conditions: hedge payoffs differ by crisis type

added_claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
added_claims.quote: if you gave me that product with a zero sharp ratio I'd still buy it
added_claims.claim: Model guides say crisis alpha plus low correlation is so valuable that an allocator would hold the product even at zero Sharpe, so the positive 0.34 Sharpe is a bonus on top of the diversification case.
added_claims.direction: include in efficient frontier on correlation

added_claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
added_claims.quote: the hedge fund sharp ratio question is a mess because there's enormous amount of selection bias
added_claims.claim: Comparing CTAs with hedge fund Sharpe ratios (for example Millennium above 2 for 30 years) is misleading because of selection bias and non-marking; being placed in the hedge fund bucket makes a 0.34 net Sharpe look disappointing.

added_claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
added_claims.quote: needs to be in vehicles like ETFs and mutual funds that then should be compared because of the liquidity and accessibility
added_claims.claim: To go mainstream, CTA exposure should be offered in ETFs and mutual funds and compared with the rest of the liquid portfolio on liquidity and accessibility, not with hedge fund return targets.

added_claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
added_claims.quote: asset allocation models generally start from this is our long-term assumption about the return on cash
added_claims.claim: Capital-market assumptions are anchored on a long-term cash return that most people got wrong ten years ago, and everything else is built on it, so the output is 'somebody's call' rather than a measurement.
added_claims.testable: yes - compare past cash assumptions with realized cash

added_claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
added_claims.quote: has done about cash was 275 over time and which is which is you know respectable and the sharp and the the VA has been less than 10 which is how you get to the 34
added_claims.claim: The SG CTA index returned about cash plus 275 bp net of fees with annualized volatility below 10%, which is how the 0.34 Sharpe arises.
added_claims.indicator: SG CTA index excess return and volatility
added_claims.conditions: net of fees and trading costs

added_claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
added_claims.quote: if you ask AI, how should I construct my portfolio? It's not going to have a lot of bonds in it
added_claims.claim: He expects AI-generated portfolio advice to hold few bonds, so AI adoption by advisers and clients could accelerate the move away from 60/40.

added_claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
added_claims.quote: I say get rid of the buckets and figure out what actually adds value and why
added_claims.claim: In a total-portfolio approach the buckets are dropped and each holding must justify its marginal value, which favors CTAs if their diversification and crisis alpha are explained in those terms.

added_claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
added_claims.quote: asset allocation portfolios. They're wonderful but they're very slow. And so you bring in something like manage it can just it can increase your ability to be more adaptive in the markets
added_claims.claim: Static allocation portfolios are slow (the sloth metaphor); managed futures adds an adaptive element as markets move faster, which is the broad pitch for including tactical exposure.

added_claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
added_claims.quote: it's like the entire equity markets have become one crazy venture capital play
added_claims.claim: The equity market has become one large venture-capital style play on AI, and a strategy that is working this year because it does things investors cannot do on their own offers a hedge to that concentration.

added_claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
added_claims.quote: they will even ask are you using a 20-day moving average and even though I'm thinking in my head you don't need to know it's completely diff it's completely irrelevant they still ask
added_claims.claim: Due-diligence questionnaires push managers into irrelevant details (such as the exact moving average), and consultants and institutional allocators expect it, so going into the weeds is a necessary evil even if it does not help long-run outcomes.

added_claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
added_claims.quote: Their technical sophistication is also part of their social identification as being a smart sophisticated allocator
added_claims.claim: Institutional manager-selection teams fill a bucket and take identity from technical sophistication, so growth will not come from them (they already own the space); it must come from simpler stories for committees, advisers and wealth clients.

added_claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
added_claims.quote: they're doing it because in their job, they like it, right? There's something about adding that to their portfolio that is going to shine back on them in some fashion
added_claims.claim: Allocators add an alternative product when it reflects well on them professionally (clients thank them later, careers advance), so the pitch should give them a story they can use, not just statistics.

added_claims.speaker: Andrew Beer
added_claims.quote: the cool position for them was to dump on the space because so many people had had these experiences
added_claims.claim: By the late 2010s and early 2020s it was fashionable among allocators to dump on managed futures after their own bad experiences (concentrating in one fund, bad timing), a sentiment trough that preceded the strong 2022 and 2026 results.
added_claims.direction: contrarian: negative sentiment preceded strong returns
added_claims.testable: partly - sentiment proxies vs subsequent returns
